newsitem.title: UK: More African women found with resistance to AIDS.
newsitem.headline: More African women found with resistance to AIDS.

text.p: Kenyan and Canadian doctors reported on Friday they had found a group of prostitutes in Nairobi who seemed stubbornly resistant to the HIV virus that causes AIDS.

It is the second study to find a group of Africans who can resist the virus. The researchers said the women did not seem to have the same genetic mutation as some Caucasians shown to be resistant to infection.
Francis Plummer and colleagues at the University of Manitoba studied 424 prostitutes in Nairobi between 1985 and 1994.

All were free of HIV infection at the beginning of the study. During the 10 years 239 of them seroconverted, or started to produce antibodies to HIV as the immune system started reacting. Most of the rest were infected to some degree.
But 43 never became infected, despite what must have been repeated exposures to the virus, Plummer's group wrote in a report in the Lancet medical journal.
"Women followed up for the entire 10-year period of our study would have experienced about 500 unprotected exposures to HIV," they wrote.
Highly sensitive tests including polymerase chain reaction (PCR), used to multiply any viral DNA, indicated they were not infected to any degree.
"Although these women could have had a cryptic HIV infection in lymph nodes or some other site, undetectable by available methods, this possibility seems unlikely," they said.
In August, U.S. doctors reported they had identified a genetic mutation that made about one percent of Caucasians studied resistant to HIV infection.

But this mutation has not been found in the African population, or among Japanese, and scientists think black Americans who have the mutation probably inherited it through an ancestor of European descent.
Two years ago British doctors reported a similar group of resistant Gambian prostitutes, and Plummer's group published interim results of their study in Nairobi in 1993.
They said once it was discovered why the African women resisted infection, the knowledge could be used to develop a vaccine or a treatment for AIDS.
